articles.title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
articles.summary:
Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi.
Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.
Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.
At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.
There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.
Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).
When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.
We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.
You can get started with `npm create factory`.
It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!

articles.title: This Week in Source Control: 18 November 2026
articles.summary:
This week’s version control and forge news, gathered from release feeds for source control clients and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News, and my boosts on Mastodon. Package management news is in the Saturday This Week in Package Management roundup.
Releases
Gerrit 3.15.0 declares Git’s reftable ref storage ready for production after load testing and fixes to the remaining stability and conversion bugs. Administrators can convert a repository between the files and reftable formats from the project screen, as long as the repository receives no writes during the conversion.
A new POST /projects/{project-name}/branches/{branch-id}/commit REST endpoint creates, updates, deletes or renames files on a branch in one commit, with no clone and no change. The caller needs Push access on the branch. An optional base_revision makes the request fail with 409 Conflict if the branch has moved.
Comments and votes can now be marked as AI-generated through an is_ai field, and the UI shows an icon next to them. The aiReview permission moves to a default-deny ACL. An experimental Stack Diff dialog shows the combined diff of a whole relation chain against its base. Gerrit is now built with JDK 25 and Bazel 9, and plugins that declare dependencies in external_plugin_deps.bzl have to move to Bazel modules.
GitButler 0.23.4 narrows its warning for repositories using Git LFS or git-crypt to editing and resolving commits. Auto-merge now works in GitHub repositories that only allow squash or rebase merges. New installs open the native app by default. In that app, a plain git commit on gitbutler/workspace no longer breaks the project, and the app offers to uncommit it and keep the changes.
Also out: Gerrit 3.14.6, 3.13.11 and 3.12.12.
Security
Gitea 28.4.0 lists 21 CVEs, including one in Go’s net/http fixed by building with Go 1.27.4 and two already fixed in earlier 28.x releases. Among them:
CVE-2026-125423: a repository created with auto-init accepted pushes before initialisation had finished. A user allowed to create repositories could push a crafted tree so that writing the README followed a symlink and overwrote a server-side git hook, which ran commands as the Gitea system user.
CVE-2026-123006: since 28.0.0 the dashboard’s repository search returned each repository’s commit status object with the owner’s full user record. Any signed-in user could read the password hash, salt and email address of the owner of any visible repository with a commit status.
CVE-2026-123638: protected file patterns were matched against file names as git prints them. Git quotes names containing a double quote, backslash or control character, so those names matched no pattern and a user with write access could change files under a protected path.
CVE-2026-118535: a repository registered as an owner-level source of scoped workflows kept that registration after a transfer. The new owner could change workflows that still ran in the previous owner’s repositories with their Actions secrets.
CVE-2026-129337: a repository still being created by a migration, fork or template has no server-side hooks, so a user with read access could push to it over HTTP during that window.
CVE-2026-123002: Gitea accepted unlimited wrong TOTP passcodes. Five failures now block further attempts on the account for 15 minutes.
GitHub Desktop 3.6.11 updates its bundled Git to 2.56.1, the release that fixed the six vulnerabilities covered last week.
GitHub
Issue types and issue fields are generally available on repositories owned by personal accounts. Each account can define up to 25 types and 25 fields under Planning in its settings, and both are exposed through the REST and GraphQL APIs and webhooks. Labels and milestones can now also be created from the issue page when a search finds no match.
The dashboard is more compact after feedback that the new default layout showed too little. Pull request and issue lists show six items by default instead of three, long titles stay on one line, and either the Feed or Home tab can be pinned as the default view. The agent sessions section is hidden for accounts with no agent sessions.
Event Streams, in preview behind a waitlist on all plans, lets a client subscribe to a pull request and keep a connection open. GitHub then sends an event when a review is submitted, commits are pushed, a merge conflict appears, a check suite changes status, or the pull request is merged or closed. Events arrive over the connection the client opened, in place of a public webhook endpoint, and the changelog presents it as a replacement for agents polling the API from a laptop.
Secret scanning has a new detector for Cloudflare service tokens, listed as cloudflare_access_service_token. Partner secrets found in public repositories are reported to the issuer, and user secrets raise alerts in public and private repositories.
Elsewhere
Git considers voting to determine its LLM policy (Jonathan Corbet, LWN) reports on a draft voting process that Emily Shaffer posted to the Git list on 21 October. Git’s contribution guidelines have said since October 2025 that anything that looks AI-generated will be rejected. A session at the Git Contributor’s Summit revisited that policy and reached no consensus.
Under the draft, proposals are patches to the project’s documentation and need a second from another eligible voter. Discussion runs for around four weeks, followed by a two-week vote. The draft gives a vote to anyone with a commit merged to next or two code reviews. Patrick Steinhardt suggested a threshold of 25 or 30 commits. The counting method is undecided, and Steinhardt and brian m. carlson both asked for a secret ballot.
Migrating from GitHub to Codeberg (Yorick Peterse) covers moving Inko and a set of personal repositories by hand with Forgejo’s repository migration feature. The GitHub importer stalled for about an hour at rate limits without reporting it, and it does not map users, so assignees had to be set again. GitHub issue types have no Forgejo equivalent and became labels.
CI moved to Forgejo Actions on self-hosted runners, because Codeberg’s shared runners are AMD64 Linux only and time-limited. Peterse reports that a git push typically takes between 5 and 10 seconds, and that a request to raise the Inko organisation’s 1.5 GiB quota was unanswered at the time of writing.
Codeberg reported on the morning of 18 November that codeberg.org was unreachable. The site is unavailable at the time of writing and the issue is ongoing. Codeberg said the domain had not expired or been transferred, but was missing from its registrar account and in clientHold status, and that no email notification had arrived. A follow-up said no warning had arrived under the registrar’s abuse reporting procedures and that a technical issue was the most likely cause.
Stacked diffs with Maiao (kqr, Entropic Thoughts) describes keeping one commit per change on a single dev branch and publishing it to GitHub with the community fork of Maiao. One git review command fetches upstream, rebases the branch, pushes a disposable branch for each commit, and opens a pull request for each as a native GitHub stack. Running it again after amending a commit force-pushes the branches and updates the pull request descriptions and merge targets.
Git Beyond the Basics (Christian Hofstede-Kuhn) is a long tutorial for people who already use add, commit and push, checked against Git 2.56.1. It covers a starting configuration, rerere, the reflog, fixup commits with autosquash, --update-refs for stacked branches, and what worktrees share.
In the signing section’s tests, a plain git rebase or git cherry-pick of a signed commit dropped the signature from the copy, and Forgejo’s “require signed commits” branch protection rejects the result. Passing -S or setting commit.gpgsign signs the new commits. Hofstede-Kuhn’s own signatures come from an OpenPGP smartcard through oct-git in place of GnuPG.
mini.nvim, the library of Neovim modules, now has mirrors on Tangled and Codeberg. Its README lists the GitHub repository as the main one.
rbit is a self-hosted Git forge written in Rust that runs as one binary with SQLite, redb and bare Git repositories in a single data directory. It reads repositories in-process with gitoxide and serves Git over smart HTTP and a built-in SSH server that offers no shell. The feature list covers issues, pull requests, reviews, Git LFS, mirrors, and imports from GitHub and Gitea. Actions jobs run on a separate rbit-runner.
GitHub processed four DMCA notices from Nintendo dated 6 November, IGN reports (Jacqueline Thomas). They target the Switch emulators Yuzu and Citron Neo and firmware for mod chips. Because the firmware’s fork network was larger than 100 repositories, GitHub applied one notice to all 144 repositories in it.
Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.

articles.title: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
articles.summary:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime (https://maritime.sh). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents.
Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY
There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is:
You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins.
It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem.
We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction:
1. Agent lifecycle management.
There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime.
There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up.
2. Custom environments.
Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies.
Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely.
3. Cost optimization.
If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure.
So what did we build differently?
We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents.
We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency.
As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed.
Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research.
We want your feedback.
If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build.
Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing?
Happy to answer any questions in the comments.
https://maritime.sh

articles.title: Are vibe-coded games making me a substance dualist?
articles.summary:
Seeing vibe-coded videogames lately makes me feel weird. The uncanny valley effect isn't "almost real but not quite" which is the case with AI-generated photos and videos. It's "almost human but not quite". And this is what makes me feel weird. What makes a video game more human?
I'm not religious nor really spiritual, but seeing those AI-generated games in action feels soulless in the most explicit way. As if there is literally an absence of soul?
You feel it when a piece of art, regardless of the technical mastery of the artist, or style, or scale, just assures you it came from someone who, like yourself, has had experiences and emotions. It may be a kid's first drawing or a grand symphony, something in it leaves you doubtless about the presence of the ineffable "soul" or whatever you want to call it. 
Funny how even inorganic nature, the landscapes, and rocks, and rivers, can feel the same even though there is nothing human, nothing even cellular behind them.
The rationalist in me can provide a meaningful explanation involving evolutionary traits and pattern recognition. Though one can simply choose to see "the soul", and it's fine, it's just how we name things that we can't quite define but mostly agree upon when we experience it.
I never felt the need to go be all woo-woo when describing stuff produced by machines, until I saw vibe-coded videogames. 
This recent video by Second Wind "How to Spot AI Art in Games" talks about assets (models, textures, etc.). Some people quickly recognize there is something "wrong", and the video explains common sources of that feeling: wrongly baked lighting, inconsistent structures, bugged out skeletons and more. So, obviously, there is a rational explanation: it feels soulless because it's literally wrong, within the ruleset of the simulated world.
But often I see vibe-coded videogames with pretty decent graphics, where I can't point a finger at very obvious faults. Stuff like this first-person shooter Saltline:

I wanted to test Fable 5.2's quality with one-shot prompts without human feedback.

Everything in this game is from scratch: models, sounds, textures. ~$550 at API pricing, ~2.7M output and 445M input tokens, heavily cached. Took 8 hours!
Play it here: https://t.co/fazOCcyNIH https://t.co/GoCitQ9EVe
— Felix Rieseberg (@felixrieseberg) November 9, 2026

Yet it plays and controls and sounds so utterly soulless. I feel like I'm in the Plato's cave looking at high-fidelity shadows on a high-fidelity cave wall, while also knowing that those shadows are cast by real things: people's art used as training data.
Some demoes are presented as impressive, but result in deep dread.

Internal test game created by a single (senior) developer in 5 days using our new tools and engine. Uses WASM mini-engine (ECS, rendering, animations and physics). 100% AI generated assets using our new asset pipeline. Custom character controller. Slop or not? https://t.co/DGSTEIcniH
— Sebastian Aaltonen (@SebAaltonen) June 8, 2026
Or this:

There are so many of them.



However, I'm pretty sure:
What I describe is not significant, spiritual, or meaningful; it's just another combo of uncanny valley effects + an expression of sadness and angst about the regress in quality and craftsmanship.
Like CGI in movies, actually good AI-generated visual stuff is not noticeable, so obviously I'm only noticing stuff that's noticeable. (Why CG Sucks (Except It Doesn't))
Small sprinkles of actual, meaningful human attention can change a vibe-coded game completely. At the moment, people who are the loudest about vibe-coding games mostly have bad taste and they seem to actually believe those results look good. 
There is no way back.

articles.title: Pluralistic: Enshittifiers groom us for scammers (18 Nov 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links Enshittifiers groom us for scammers: The harder it is to tell a scam from a shitty business practice, the easier life gets for scammers. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Fannish accent; Photoshopping culture; Sixth HHGTTG novel discovers; Dragon sausages must contain dragon; Tumblr users melt Congress's phones; Pizza is a vegetable; Fake news author is a "satirist"; Trump wants a seawall around his golf resort (even though climate change is a "hoax"); "Nimona"; Harvard v meritocracy; Disney loses Roger Rabbit. Upcoming appearances: Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Enshittifiers groom us for scammers (permalink) We live in a scam economy: there's a presidential memecoin, a public health system run by a supplement peddler (who sold his trademark for "MAHA" to a pal before taking the job), and Spacex got to debut into the NASDAQ 100 and turn your retirement savings into exit liquidity for Musk's Emirati and tech oligarch cronies: https://prospect.org/2026/06/10/elon-musk-spacex-ipo-retirement-savings-index-funds-stock-market/#:~:text=The%20upcoming%20SpaceX,rake%20in%20millions. Then there's AI: voice cloning, deepfakes, and image-genned documents (including convincing IDs) have ushered in a golden age of account takeovers, identity theft and good, old-fashioned impersonation: https://www.404media.co/the-confessions-of-an-ai-fraud-kingpin-onlyfake-owner-nazarenko/ AI summarization is a priceless gift to fraudsters, who can comb through otherwise intractable mountains of breach data to customize precision-targeted spear-phishing campaigns for millions of potential victims at once. These summarization tools have a lot to summarize, thanks to a string of catastrophic breaches that saw (for example) the escape of the credit histories of nearly every person in America: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Equifax_data_breach The companies involved in those breaches were not meaningfully punished. Quite the contrary, they were allowed to buy up and merge more of their competitors, combining these new divisions' creaking servers with their own spit-and-baling-wire frankensystems, even as they fired the people who had built and maintained those systems (in the name of "efficiency"). The commercial surveillance sector has repeatedly proven itself to be more interested in profits than security or accuracy, and yet we continue to entrust them with crucial public functions, including purging electoral rolls: https://mississippitoday.org/2026/11/10/u-s-senate-election-mississippi-andrew-goodman/ For margin-obsessed corporate leadership, IT cuts represent a unique hazard. When a manager fires the person who maintains the assembly line, the shop-floor quickly seizes up. But managers who fire IT staff inherit software that keeps chugging along long after the people who built it are gone…until it stops, and the company no longer knows how to restart it. This is one of the unique challenges of unionizing tech workers: when the tech workers go on strike, the scab software they wrote crosses the picket line on them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook Tech debt has a long maturity: you can incur a lot of tech debt before the margin call comes and you find yourself in technological bankruptcy. Corporate management has spent decades playing IT Jenga, removing every available block, leaving behind a skeletal skyline of teetering towers that now routinely collapse: https://www.404media.co/breaking-everything/ The entire IT system is grossly overleveraged and technological bankruptcies are everywhere. This is very bad, because the USA hasn't had a new consumer privacy law since 1988 (when Congress banned disclosure of your VHS rental history), which means that these eggshell-thin servers are jammed with the most sensitive data imaginable about everyone, everywhere: https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/02/agony-verification/#great-turnbulls-ghost Far from breaking this cycle of overaccumulation and breach of sensitive data, the AI sector is accelerating it, claiming that a single person's "consent" to use pervert glasses, always-on mics, or other surveillance equipment can stand in for the consent of everyone they meet, see, or converse with: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/tech-companies-are-trying-shift-entire-concept-privacy-again This is the new normal: everything is broken, everything is breached. It's completely normal to wake up and read panicked headlines advising companies to shut off their servers until the latest showstopper bug can be patched. Half the email you get is from companies announcing new security protocols in the wake of a fresh data breach (the other half is from companies announcing changes to their terms of service to allow them to collect even more of your data, and to ban you from suing them when that data leaks): https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/26/abandon-hope/#all-ye-who-enter-here So it's also normal to get phone calls, emails and texts from your bank, employer, insurer and broker asking you to verify a transaction or requiring you to sign up for a new two-factor authentication system. What's more, it's normal for these entities to insist that you immediately install a new app or go through a new authentication process that is totally unlike any of the other ones you're already using. It's normal to log in to a service you use every day and be confronted with an entirely different login flow – a CAPTCHA unlike any you've ever seen, a requirement to visit a third-party site to complete an authentication step (which may involve taking selfies and transmitting copies of sensitive ID documents using an app from a company you've never heard of), an embedded widget that only works if you disable your browser's advanced privacy settings that prevent cross-site scripting and other horrors. We're told to hang up on anyone who calls us from our bank or credit-card issuer and to call them back using the number on the back of our cards. But when we call our banks, we get shunted to AI chatbots that "hallucinate" nonsensical advice for accessing our accounts. If we try to reach a human, we're stuck in lengthy hold queues whose soundtrack is a looping announcement scolding us for not using a faulty chatbot or the company's broken website to solve our problems. When a human does come on the line, they often seem to be improvising a new security protocol that was created five minutes before to deal with the latest state of exception. This is the security storm: a world of zero visibility, shifting gale-force winds, and blockages that impede your usual route and force you down unfamiliar paths every time you venture forth. It is the perfect environment for fraudsters. It's not just that fraudsters can impersonate anyone with AI voice-cloning or generate undetectable document forgeries: it's also the fact that your bank, HR department, insurer, credit card company and government have groomed you to expect a chaotic process that requires you to do something different every time you try to access a service. They've groomed you to turn off your browser's advanced protections. They've groomed you to ignore your carefully created, carefully saved random passwords in favor of clicking on links that get texted or emailed to you by third-party services you've never heard of. They've groomed you to expect cold-calls from outsource fraud prevention companies that don't know how to pronounce your bank's name. This isn't new. As far back as 2009, the cryptographer Ben Laurie was railing against "Verified by Visa," which required you to enter sensitive data into a page hosted on a domain that was separate from both your bank and the merchant you were paying, which Laurie called "Phished by Visa": https://web.archive.org/web/20090331094020/http://www.links.org/?p=591 No one listened to Laurie. Instead, the banks got worse. I've been a customer of HSBC subsidiary Firstdirect for nearly 20 years, and in that time, I've been told to make note of a "customer ID number," a "telephone passcode", eight password recovery answers, a "web username", a web password, a "digital secure key password", a "digital secure key PIN", and a regular PIN. Despite all this, I haven't been able to access my bank account for two months, ever since they "upgraded" their system to block app log-ins on mobile devices running the open, secure Android fork Graphene (Firstdirect doesn't use a standard two-factor authenticator; you have to use its app to generate a one-time PIN in addition to all those other authentication details every time you log in, even via a browser). When I spoke to Firstdirect about why they'd blocked Graphene, they told me that they "considered open source to be insecure." Talk about grooming for fraudsters: telling your customers that they should only trust systems that can't be independently inspected and validated is grossly irresponsible. (Don't worry, we're going to use the UK's excellent open banking system to switch back to the Co-Op Bank, which we left after it was mismanaged to the brink of bankruptcy and flogged to private equity; it's since been restructured as a co-op again:) https://www.banktrack.org/success/the_cooperative_bank_bought_back_into_mutual_ownership The perfect mark is someone who thinks they can't get scammed. The more technologically savvy and security conscious you are, the more you've encountered the incoherence of the official system and the less surprised you'll be when you're told to do something obviously insecure in order to complete a transaction: Boy, that stupid, dangerous requirement is even stupider and more dangerous than all the other stupid, dangerous things I've been forced to do this year. That's the story of Uri Bram, a technological sophisticate who edits Atoms vs Bits and nearly got scammed trying to buy an Amtrak ticket: https://www.atvbt.com/expected-incompetence-enables-fraud/ Bram tried to buy his Amtrak ticket on the web but found himself on a nonfunctional site that put him through a bizarre stopgap process that required him to enter his email address, click a link, log in to his Paypal account… Each step was more out-of-place than the last, but all of them had the eerie ring of plausibility, given the dysfunction of Bram's other interactions with giant, creaking companies like Amtrak. As Bram puts it: "Expected incompetence enables fraud." The corollary is that technological excellence makes fraud easier to spot and harder to pull off. Most of our anti-fraud measures demand that you be more vigilant and more discerning. We'd be much better off if we insisted that our official institutions invest in coherent, orderly practices that are thoughtfully designed, well maintained, and staffed by easily reached experts who can guide us through our problems. It's much harder to impersonate a system where you can get through to a thoroughly trained, in-house customer service rep in a few minutes than it is to impersonate a system that's typically worse than the fraudster's vibe-coded scam website, whose "customer service" has been replaced by broken chatbots. The ongoing collapse of all of our technology has created a permanent state of exception in which fraudsters' demands are no weirder than the ad-libbing our own essential institutions engage in every time we deal with them. The answer can't be to demand superhuman fraud-detection skills from the public: rather, we must demand excellence from our institutions: articles.title: Jensen Huang Tweets
articles.summary:
Jensen Huang, on X yesterday, hours before Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report:
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from
NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers
for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me
directly as the company navigates complex technology, market,
competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a
once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides
that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our
employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer
these calls and return as CEO.
Doing this in public is pathetic. There are in fact a lot of simps out there — largely on X — clamoring for Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang. Here, for example, is Jason Calacanis, who works as David Sacks’s pool boy:
China Hawks are going to get a chip ban, and Americans are going to get a recession.
To believe Calacanis, the only thing holding up the entire U.S. economy is Nvidia’s chip sales into China in violation of national security law. This, too, is a pathetic opinion to express in public.
All of these bring-back-Jensen stans are stuck in the denial stage of grief. The national security China hawks won. It’s over. Huang is out, done in by his own staggering hubris. Huang’s miscalculation was that after his side lost the debate over what U.S. national security policy should be regarding AI chip sales to China, he wrongly presumed Nvidia could just ignore the spirit, if not the letter, of the law and just sell banned Nvidia chips into China anyway, because he had Trump on his side. That cronyism had won out, and if you had Trump on your side, you could do whatever you wanted. People who think this way often overestimate the permanence of their erosions of the rule of law and liberal democracy. The Nazis thought the Third Reich would last 1,000 years — it lasted 12.
Turns out U.S. national security officials still run U.S. national security policy. Turns out Democrats weren’t out of power in Congress for long.

articles.title: ★ The 50-Yard Line
articles.summary:
Ever since the Huang/Nvidia scandal erupted, I’ve been thinking about a short post I wrote back in March, under the headline “Jensen Huang Doesn’t Smell Anything”:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, during an on-stage interview at The Hill
& Valley Forum last week, was asked “What do you see as America’s
unique advantages that other countries don’t have?”
His answer, after taking a moment to think, “America’s unique
advantage that no country could possibly have is President Trump.”
Huang, newly appointed to the aforelinked President’s Council
of Advisors on Science and Technology, seemingly doesn’t smell
the growing stink.
The stink was the historically low (and sinking) popularity to which Trump’s 2.0 presidency had sunk, just one year in. Undeniable to anyone in touch with reality. Huang’s obsequious Trump-fellating answer to that question would have been eye-catching even a year prior, when Trump first rolled back into office with an aggressive agenda and a surplus of political capital from a clear election victory — but it was, frankly, a startling thing to say in March 2026. It makes a lot more sense, though, given what’s come to light in the last 10 days.
If you’re not paying close attention you might think Huang’s was the sort of answer any major tech CEO might have given. But it’s not. That was a really unusual thing for Huang to say, way out of line with how corporate leaders typically approach politics. The typical approach for large publicly held corporations is to avoid partisan politics. Advocate only for policies directly related to the company’s business, and otherwise stay out. The political winds change direction every few years. George Bush senior in 1988 was the last new president elected from the same party as the outgoing incumbent, and he only lasted one term. It makes no sense for a corporation that intends to continue thriving for more than the next few years to closely align itself with one party — unless they believe that party will remain in power for the foreseeable future, à la the FDR/Truman Democrats, who won five consecutive presidential elections from 1932 to 1948 (and seven out of nine through 1968).
One metaphor I use for politics is a football field. Democrats on the left, Republicans on the right. CEOs typically stay as close as they can to the 50-yard line in the middle of the field. That way, when an election puts the other party in power, they don’t have to move — they just need to turn around. That’s how someone like Tim Cook could maintain good relations with the White House from Obama to Trump to Biden back to Trump again. He just stayed close to midfield and turned around after each election.
Remaining as close as possible to political midfield under Trump required unseemly obsequious tribute, unprecedented in modern U.S. history. Million-dollar tickets to his inauguration. That ridiculous gold trophy. Embarrassing stuff. But that’s ultimately a reflection of Trump’s avarice, not the politics of Cook personally or Apple as a company. That was the price to stay on the 50-yard line. Cook has often repeated that his two personal heroes are Martin Luther King Jr. and Bobby Kennedy (senior, to be clear). He keeps portraits of both of them in his office. He never swapped them out for portraits of, say, Ronald Reagan. Apple never changed its internal policies or language regarding racial and LGBT equality. The Apple homepage never stopped celebrating Martin Luther King Jr. Day — even when it coincided with Trump’s second inauguration.
And yet Trump remains so enamored of Cook that he floated his name to succeed Huang at Nvidia. Tim Apple remains the apple of Trump’s eye. Yet Apple had nothing to change or apologize for when Biden came into office, nor will they again if, as now seems likely, Trump is succeeded in 2029 by a Democrat elected to clean up his kakistocratic kleptomaniacal mess. (Presumably Apple will gladly pony up at least another $25 million to restore the East Wing after Trump’s architecturally ungodly ballroom edifice is torn down.) And Apple certainly won’t need lawyers to defend them from charges of corruption and/or breaches of national security. Nvidia, not so much.
This is what we should want: business leaders who endeavor to stay out of partisan politics, not hopelessly enmesh themselves in it. Industry and politics cannot operate in isolation, but they should avoid intertwinement except where necessary. Great companies stand the test of time. That’s not feasible if you hitch your corporate wagon to one party or the other, no matter the political moment. We don’t think of Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola, or Berkshire Hathaway as being Democratic or Republican companies. You cannot chart their fortunes over time based on which party was in power in any given decade. You may well have strong political opinions that are far from the 50-yard line, on one side or the other. I do. But you shouldn’t look for those opinions to be validated by industry executives, any more than you should look for business and product-design decisions to be made by elected government officials. True American values put country over party when it comes to business. And, as Calvin Coolidge aptly put it, “The chief business of the American people is business.”
America does possess unique advantages that other countries don’t have. Personal liberties enshrined in our Bill of Rights. A vibrant, diverse, ever-changing melting pot of a citizenry. A strong tradition of the rule of law, placing no man above it. Competitive markets that allow new entrants to supplant entrenched incumbents. Any CEO worth their salt should have an answer to the question of America’s unique advantages that holds true no matter who, from which party, is currently president. And they should believe it.
What makes Huang’s answer so off-putting isn’t that it was so abjectly partisan — politically tone-deaf to the inevitability of Democrats coming back into power, and perversely obsequious to Trump personally — but that Donald Trump is the antithesis to the entire above list of things that actually give America unique advantages other countries don’t have. Trump and the MAGA movement are also decidedly American and uniquely so, but they represent what’s worst about America.
But I give Huang credit for honesty. Clearly, he believed what he said. Huang didn’t just stray from the 50-yard line — he broke for Trump’s end zone.
